title: Choosing a Teaching Point and Writing the Aim
brief: Walk the reader through selecting a single, concrete teaching point as the foundation of the lesson, then show how to turn it into a clear lesson objective. Draw on the source's description of the Lesson Plan Template, which asks teachers to specify 'lesson objectives' and 'skill/content focus areas,' and on the Bloom's Taxonomy handout description, which states that the taxonomy provides 'verbs that can be used to describe each category' and helps teachers make 'lesson objectives.' Use the worked-example framing to narrate why a vague aim ('do vocabulary') is less useful than a focused, verb-driven one, and explain how the chosen teaching point will shape every subsequent decision in the plan.

title: Mapping the Skill Areas and Integrating Language Skills
brief: Show how the lesson plan template's 'skill/content focus areas' field prompts the teacher to think beyond a single skill and consider integration. Draw directly on the source's repeated references to 'integrated language skills' as a video focus in Unit 10 and on the Unit 9 action-plan prompt, which asks teachers to 'integrate the four skills (reading, writing, speaking, listening), grammar, and vocabulary.' Use the worked example to narrate how a teacher decides which skills are primary and which are secondary for the chosen teaching point, and why making that decision early prevents the lesson from feeling scattered.

title: Sequencing Activities: From Warm-Up to Main Task
brief: Narrate the process of ordering activities within the lesson, using the source's concept of 'lesson sequencing' named in the Lesson Plan Template description. Draw on the K-W-L Chart description (a 'warm-up activity with a reflection follow-up component' that encourages learners to think about what they know, what they want to know, and what they have learned) as a concrete example of how a warm-up can activate prior knowledge and set up the main task. Also draw on the source's description of the Mad Lib activity as a 'fun vocabulary and/or grammar activity completed in pairs or small groups' to illustrate how a warm-up can be both engaging and purposeful. Narrate the choices the teacher makes at each transition point.

title: Timing, Flexibility, and Staying on Task
brief: Address the practical challenge of managing time within the sequence, drawing on the source's explicit discussion of timing: 'the teacher decides to let the discussion continue during the oral retelling of the story' and the follow-up question 'How can this choice affect the rest of your lesson plan?' Use this to narrate how a teacher builds in flexible timing rather than rigid minute-by-minute slots. Also draw on the source's classroom-management material about students being 'off task: standing when they should be sitting, not following directions, or talking out of turn,' and the techniques teachers use 'to manage the off-task students without disrupting the flow of the lesson,' to show how timing decisions and management decisions are linked.

title: Wrapping Up and Checking Objectives
brief: Guide the reader through designing the lesson's closing stage, drawing on the source's 'Wrap-Up' section, which asks why a teacher might 'include movement in this stage of the lesson' and describes the last activity as a deliberate pedagogical choice rather than an afterthought. Connect the wrap-up directly back to the objectives by drawing on the source's 'Objectives and Assessment' section, which asks whether the teacher 'formally or informally assessed student performance or knowledge' and how the teacher 'evaluated whether the objectives were met during the lesson.' Narrate how the worked-example teacher chooses a closing activity that doubles as informal assessment of the lesson's teaching point.

title: Reviewing, Sharing, and Revising the Plan
brief: Show the reader that a finished draft is not a finished plan, drawing on the source's action-plan cycle, which instructs teachers to 'share your lesson plan with colleagues and get feedback, revise your plan as needed,' then 'try your plan or part of your plan in class' and 'reflect on what went well and what you might do differently.' Draw also on the source's peer-feedback and self-assessment resources — the Discussion Leader Self-Assessment Worksheet, Peer Assessment Worksheet, and the self-editing and peer-editing station instructions — as models of the same reflective loop applied to student work, showing that the habit of review the teacher builds into the lesson is the same habit the teacher should apply to the plan itself.
